ideal: Rad1 allows Nh3+ Qxh3 Bxh3, when the mate threat on g2 forces Rxd5 exd5, costing a rook for a knight.
note: Qxh3 is forced, and the mate threat explains why White must surrender the exchange after trading queens.

ideal: Rg8 allows Bxf7+ Ke7 Bxg8 Qxg8, losing the g8-rook and f7-pawn for a bishop.
note: The bishop forks king and rook; losing castling rights is incidental to the material loss.

ideal: Qe7 misses Bxf3 gxf3 Nd4, followed by Nxf3+, winning the pawn on f3 with check and costing White castling.
note: The knight and bishop exchange evenly, leaving a pawn won and a king forced to move.

ideal: Qxd6 allows Rxd5: the mate threat on h7 prevents recapture, and ...f5 Rxd6 fxe4 Rxe6 wins a bishop and knight for a pawn.
note: The h7 mate threat makes the rook capture work; the queens subsequently cancel out.

ideal: bxc7 misses Nc3, threatening mate on b5 and meeting ...Qe1+ with Rg1, followed by ...Qxg1+ Kxg1.
note: The b5 mate threat is immediate; the queen-for-rook-and-knight exchange is part of Black's counterchecking line.

ideal: Qh5 allows ...Nxc2+ Kd1 Nxa1, losing the a1-rook to a knight fork.
note: The rook fork is the main loss; the king move is a consequence of the check.

ideal: Bf1 allows ...Nc2+ Kd1 Nxa1, losing the a1-rook.
note: White also moves the king in the best line, so castling rights do not explain the difference.

ideal: h6 allows Nd5 Qg6 Nc7+, followed by Nxa8, costing a rook for a knight.
note: The king-rook fork wins the exchange, with the knight eventually recaptured on a8.

ideal: a6 allows Nxc7+ Kf7 Nxe6 Kxe6 Bxa6, losing a bishop and two pawns for a knight.
note: The subsequent pawn exchange changes neither the net two-pawn loss nor the bishop-for-knight trade.

ideal: Kc1 allows ...Rxc2+ and ...Nxb2+, starting checks that win the h1-rook; Nxa8 instead permits Rd1 with a mate threat on d8.
note: Both lines take a8, but the best line gains a defensive tempo with Rd1 rather than allowing the checking knight tour.

ideal: e5 allows Nxh7, taking the h7-pawn with a mate threat on f8.
note: Nxh7 both wins a pawn and protects the queen's mating capture on f8, prompting ...Rg8.

ideal: Nxe4 misses Ng4 and ...Qh4, threatening mate on h2 and taking f2 after h3.
note: The attack on h2 is the main point, and the f2 capture is part of its continuation.

ideal: gxf4 loses the f6-knight to exf6+ and allows Qg7 with a mate threat on h8.
note: The knight loss and the ensuing mating attack are both real, but the material loss already gives a fair reason.

ideal: Qxf7 allows ...gxh3, threatening mate on g2 and meeting Kf1 with ...Bxg3 and a new mate threat on f2.
note: The queen is given up as a delaying check after the mating attack has already taken over.

ideal: Qe7 misses Qe8, which trades queens and answers Nxh6 with ...Nxc2+ and ...Nxa1, winning a rook and pawn for a knight.
note: The h6-knight is the compensation for the a1-rook and c2-pawn; castling loss is incidental.

ideal: g5 misses Rg5+, which wins the b7-pawn and reaches Rxf8 with a mate threat on e8.
note: The rook trade leaves a net pawn gain, but the continuing mating attack is the stronger explanation.

ideal: Nc5 allows Nxb6, when the mate threat on f7 shields the knight until it takes the a8-rook after ...Ne6 Bxe6 fxe6.
note: The mate threat explains why the apparently capturable b6-knight survives to win the rook.

ideal: Nh4 misses Nfd4, which meets ...Bxd4 with Nxd4 and ...Rc2+ with Nxc2, winning a bishop overall.
note: The f8 mate threat only appears after the c8-rook leaves and is answered by checks; the material gain survives the full line.

ideal: O-O-O misses Nf5, threatening mate on g5 and winning the d7-knight after ...Ne5 dxe5.
note: The mate threat explains Black's otherwise surprising knight sacrifice on e5.

ideal: Rc1 allows ...Rxf2+ Kg1 Qf4, threatening mate on h2 while attacking the c1-rook.
note: Qf4 combines the mating threat with an attack on the rook, so the damage goes beyond the f2-pawn.

ideal: gxf6 opens the g-file, and after ...Qd6 White gives queen and pawn for rook and knight with Qg7+ Rxg7 fxg7+ Kxg7 to hold off the attack on g3.
note: Moving the g-pawn exposes the queen to the rook while ...Qd6 attacks g3; the later g3 mate threat is genuine.

ideal: h3 allows ...Bxh3, taking the h3-pawn while threatening mate on g2.
note: The g2-pawn is pinned, and the mating attack matters more than the single pawn gained.

ideal: Qg3 allows ...Nxe4 Qxg7 Bxf2+, forcing the king to move and eventually losing the h1-rook after ...Ng3 and ...Nxh1.
note: The pawn count is correct at Bxf2+, but the exposed king and ensuing rook loss are the main consequences.

ideal: Qxg3 misses Qxe4+ Be3 Bxe3 Bd3 Bxf2+ Kxf2, winning the e4- and f2-pawns while drawing the king out.
note: The bishops exchange evenly, and the second pawn capture comes with check and loss of castling.

ideal: Bd7 allows Bxf7+ Kxf7 Qxd7, winning the f7-pawn and drawing the king out.
note: The f7 capture deflects the king before White recovers the bishop on d7.

ideal: Bc5 leaves the c8-rook to Nxc8, followed by Qd7 with a mate threat on d8.
note: The rook is lost immediately; the genuine d8 mate threat strengthens White's follow-up.

ideal: Nd4 misses Qd5 Nf3 Bxf3 gxf3 Qxf3, winning the f3-knight and a pawn for a bishop.
note: Candidate 1 omits Rf1 Qg4, making its Ng3 illegal because it exposes the king on e1 to the queen on f3.

ideal: Nf7 allows the queen trade and ...Nxc2+ followed by ...Nxa1, losing the a1-rook and c2-pawn for the h6-knight.
note: The rook-and-pawn loss for a knight is the concrete penalty; the forced king move is incidental.

ideal: Rd1 misses Qc2 and ...h5, when ...exf3 answers f4 with a mate threat on g2.
note: The en passant pawn gain is temporary, whereas clearing f2 and controlling g2 explains the attack.

ideal: Bxe5 allows Nxe5 and Nd6+, drawing the king to e7 and then d6 while the d5-knight blocks the rook on d1.
note: Black recovers a knight with ...Kxd6, so a lasting bishop-for-pawn loss is misleading; the exposed king is the main issue.
